blocks.x: STAT 153 · Statistical Methods · Topic 1

Before we can describe a dataset or draw a conclusion from it, we need a shared vocabulary. This topic introduces what statistics actually is, who relies on it (especially in medicine and public health), and the core building-block concepts — IVPPSS, variables, and measurement scales — that every later topic in this course depends on.

By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Define statistics and explain the process it describes — collecting, compiling, analysing, presenting, publishing and disseminating numerical facts (data) to support informed decisions.

2Identify who uses statistics — government, businesses, researchers, health professionals, economists and policy makers — and describe real applications, especially in clinical trials, disease diagnosis and treatment, epidemiology and healthcare quality improvement.
3Distinguish Descriptive from Inferential statistics and recognise which one a given statement (e.g. hospital patient ages) is illustrating.
4Define and correctly apply IVPPSS — Individual, Variable, Population, Parameter, Sample and Statistic — to a real study scenario, and follow the six-step process for setting one up.
5Classify a variable as quantitative (discrete or continuous) or qualitative (nominal or ordinal), using medical examples.
6Identify the scale of measurement — nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio — of any given variable, and match it to the chart type appropriate for summarising it.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Statistics A scientific method of collection, compilation, analysis, presentation, publication and dissemination of numerical facts (data), carried out in order to make informed decisions. It is both a set of methods and the body of numbers those methods produce.

What statisticians actually do
Design experiments and surveys; collect and manage data; select the best method for analysing the data and making an inference for a given sampling situation; and analyse the collected data while providing a measure of how good that inference is.
Statistics→ Descriptive / Inferential→ IVPPSS→ Variables→ Measurement Scales
Why statistics exists

Statistics is not just a school subject — it is a working tool for government, business, medicine and research. This tab covers what statistics is, who uses it, where it is applied (with a close look at medicine), the software that powers real analyses, and the two fundamental types of statistics.
What is statistics?

Statistics A scientific method of collection, compilation, analysis, presentation, publication and dissemination of numerical facts (data), in order to make informed decisions. Anyone working in a data-driven field needs to understand its basic concepts as well as its strengths and limitations.
Users of statistics

Statisticians provide great assistance to scientific research by designing experiments and surveys, collecting and managing data, choosing the best method of analysis and inference for a given sampling situation, and reporting how good that inference is. The major groups that rely on this work include:

items: 1Government — for census counts, national planning, and monitoring social and economic indicators.
2Businesses — for market research, forecasting demand, and quality control.
3Researchers — across every scientific discipline, to design studies and interpret results.
4Health professionals — to evaluate treatments, track disease patterns, and improve patient care.
5Economists — to analyse markets, inflation, employment and growth trends.
6Policy makers — to design and justify legislation and public programmes using evidence.

blocks.x: Where statistics gets used
Investment decisions
Financial planners study recent trends in stock market prices to guide investment decisions for their clients.
Opinion polls
Politicians and their supporters rely heavily on public opinion poll data to formulate legislation and devise campaign strategies about their prospects of winning an election.
Water quality

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is always interested in the water quality of rivers and lakes. It periodically takes water samples to establish the level of contamination and to maintain quality.
Medicine & public health
Statistics underpins almost every stage of clinical and public-health decision making — detailed below, since this is the application area most relevant to your training.
How statistics is applied in medicine

items: 1Clinical trials: designing experiments and analysing data to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of drugs, vaccines and medical devices before they reach patients.
2Disease diagnosis and treatment: comparing treatment outcomes (for example, surgery versus therapy) to identify the most effective interventions for a given condition.
3Epidemiology: studying the distribution, causes and spread of diseases in populations to inform prevention and control strategies.
4Quality improvement: monitoring hospital performance, patient outcomes and safety indicators in order to improve the healthcare services delivered.

Descriptive vs. Inferential statistics

Descriptive statistics Statistics used to describe and summarise data — for example, "The average age of patients admitted to this hospital is 62." It tells you about the data you actually have, and nothing beyond it.

Inferential statistics The set of procedures used to make generalisations about the characteristics of a population using information contained in a sample randomly selected from the population under investigation. It lets you reach beyond the data you collected.

blocks.title: Worked contrast: the hospital patient-age example

items: Descriptive statement: "The average age of patients admitted to this hospital is 62" — this simply reports a fact calculated directly from the hospital's own records. No generalisation is being made beyond those records.

Inferential statement: "Based on a random sample of 200 patients from this hospital, we estimate that the average age of all patients ever admitted is around 62, with a margin of error of ±2 years" — here the sample's result is being used to generalise to a wider population.
The key giveaway: descriptive statistics summarise the data in hand; inferential statistics use a sample to say something about a population beyond that sample.

blocks.x: The six terms every analysis must define

Before you can understand or appreciate how statistical inference works, you must be able to tell apart population from sample and parameter from statistic — and before even that, you must identify the individual and the variable(s) of interest. These six items, together known by the acronym IVPPSS, must be explicitly identified at the start of any statistical analysis for that analysis to be done properly.
The six IVPPSS terms

Individual
The single unit (a person, patient, object or event) on which the variable is actually measured or observed.
Variable A characteristic of interest measured on individuals.
Population A collection of all possible individual units whose characteristics are to be studied.
Parameter A quantitative measure that describes a characteristic of a population. A parameter is usually unknown in practice, because measuring every member of a population is rarely feasible.
Sample A subset of the population that is studied in order to make inferences about the population.

Statistic A numerical description of a sample characteristic. Because it can actually be computed from data in hand, the statistic is used to estimate the corresponding (unknown) population parameter.
Six steps in performing IVPPSS
1. Identify Individuals→ 2. Identify Variables→ 3. Know the Population→ 4. Identify the Parameter→ 5. Select a Sample→ 6. Compute the Statistic

Population vs. Sample — the big picture The population is the entire group of interest; the sample is a subset selected from that population; and every inference we make is based on the sample, not on the (usually inaccessible) full population. A parameter is the true, fixed value that belongs to the population; a statistic is the number we actually calculate, from the sample, to estimate that parameter.
Antenatal visits in a municipality

Public health officers want to estimate the average number of antenatal visits made by pregnant women in a municipality. A random sample of 165 pregnant women is selected, and the number of antenatal visits made by each woman is recorded. Derive the IVPPSS terms from this statement.

items: IIndividualA pregnant woman
VVariableNumber of antenatal visits
PPopulationAll pregnant women in the municipality
PParameterMean number of antenatal visits among all pregnant women in the municipality
SSampleThe 165 randomly selected pregnant women
SStatisticMean number of antenatal visits of the 165 sampled women

blocks.x: Notice the pattern: the individual and variable describe what is measured and on whom; population and parameter describe the (unobserved) whole group and its true value; sample and statistic describe the (observed) subset and the value actually computed from it.
Practice: systolic blood pressure in hypertensive patients

A medical doctor at a teaching hospital wants to estimate the average systolic blood pressure of adult patients diagnosed with hypertension at the hospital. Since it is not practical to measure the blood pressure of all such patients, the doctor randomly selects 120 hypertensive patients and records their systolic blood pressure levels.

items: IIndividualAn adult patient diagnosed with hypertension
VVariableSystolic blood pressure (mmHg)
PPopulationAll adult patients diagnosed with hypertension at the hospital
PParameterMean systolic blood pressure among all hypertensive adult patients at the hospital
SSampleThe 120 randomly selected hypertensive patients
SStatisticMean systolic blood pressure of the 120 sampled patients

blocks.x: Notice that the setup is structurally identical to the antenatal-visits example — only the individuals, variable and context change. Once you can spot "a doctor wants to estimate an average for a group too large to measure fully, so a random sample is drawn instead," the six IVPPSS terms follow automatically.
What exactly are we measuring?

A variable is the information a researcher actually records about each individual. Correctly classifying a variable is not a formality — it determines which summary statistics, charts and statistical tests are valid for it later in the course.
What is a variable?

Variable The characteristic about each individual that a researcher records. Formally, a variable is a characteristic or occurrence that assumes different values or forms within a given range of values or forms, known as the domain of the variable. Examples: height, IQ, weight, body temperature.
Quantitative vs. Qualitative variables
Quantitative variables
Variables that assume measurable/quantifiable forms — they are recorded as numbers that carry numeric meaning. Examples: volume, height, number of children vaccinated.
Qualitative variables
Variables that assume forms that are only descriptive, not measurable. Synonyms for "qualitative" are "categorical" or "attribute." Examples: religion, blood group, gender, sickle cell status.
The type of variable determines the type of data produced — and, in turn, the analysis methods that will later be valid for it.
Discrete vs. Continuous
Discrete variables
Quantitative variables that have a countable number of values — you can list them 1, 2, 3… Examples: number of patients in a hospital, number of children vaccinated.
Continuous variables

Quantitative variables that have an uncountable number of values — a potential value exists between every pair of values. Examples: blood pressure (mmHg), cholesterol level (mg/dL), body temperature (°C).
Nominal vs. Ordinal
Nominal variables
Qualitative variables where no order or ranking exists among the categories. Examples: gender (male, female), blood group (A, B, AB, O).
Ordinal variables
Qualitative variables where a natural order or ranking exists among the categories. Examples: cancer stage (Stage I, II, III, IV), disease severity (low, medium, high).
Quick classification table

c: Number of patients in a hospital

items: "Number of antenatal visits made by a pregnant woman" → quantitative, and countable (you can't have 2.5 visits) → discrete.
"Systolic blood pressure of a hypertensive patient (mmHg)" → quantitative, and a value can always exist between any two readings → continuous.
"Type of treatment received (surgery, medication, therapy)" → descriptive categories with no inherent ranking → qualitative, nominal.
"Severity of injury (fatal, serious, minor, no injury)" → descriptive categories that do have a natural ranking → qualitative, ordinal.

blocks.x: How much information does the data carry?

Classifying a variable as quantitative or qualitative is only half the story. Its scale of measurement determines exactly how much information the data contains, which summary statistics are meaningful, and which chart types are appropriate for displaying it.
Measurement and scale of measurement
Measurement The application of mathematics to things or events in a meaningful and consistent way.

Scale of measurement The scale of measurement of data determines the amount of information contained in the data. It indicates which data summarisation methods and statistical analyses are most appropriate for that data. There are four scales of measurement: Nominal, Ordinal, Interval and Ratio.
Nominal scale
Nominal scale Data that represent categories, names or labels. There is no implied order to the categories of nominal data, and arithmetic operations on nominal data are inappropriate.

items: 1Type of treatment (surgery, medication, therapy)
2Gender: male or female
3Marital status: single, married, divorced
4Employment status: employed, unemployed

blocks.x: Ordinal scale

Ordinal scale Has the properties of a nominal scale, and can additionally be used to rank or order the data. Arithmetic operations still do not make sense for ordinal data — the gap between "moderate" and "bad" is not a defined numeric quantity.

items: 1Severity of injury: fatal, serious, minor, no injury
2Taste of food: good, moderate, bad
3Academic performance: excellent, very good, poor
4Cancer stage: I, II, III, IV

blocks.x: Interval scale
Interval scale Data can be ranked, and the precise differences between the ranks do exist and are meaningful; however, zero does not indicate absence of the quantity being measured.

items: 1Temperature: the difference between temperatures of 10° and 50° indicates that one is warmer than the other. However, a temperature of zero does not mean there is no temperature.
2IQ of a person: the difference between an IQ of 50 and 110 indicates that one person is more intelligent than the other. However, an IQ of zero does not mean the person has no intelligence.

blocks.x: Ratio scale

Ratio scale Possesses all the characteristics of the interval scale, but here zero means absence of the quantity — making true ratios between values meaningful (e.g. a tumour of 4 cm is genuinely twice the size of one at 2 cm).

items: 1Tumour size or volume
2Area of an ulcer or lesion
3Number of hospital visits
4Lung capacity

blocks.x: Summary of measurement scales

Reading the table: Nominal gives you categories only. Ordinal adds order. Interval adds equal intervals on top of order. Ratio adds a true (meaningful) zero on top of everything interval already has — each scale down the table carries strictly more information than the one above it.
Which chart suits which scale?
Nominal or ordinal data
Use Bar Charts (simple, multiple, compound, etc.) or Pie Charts — these display counts or proportions across categories without implying continuous measurement.
Interval or ratio data
Use a Histogram, frequency polygon, or ogive — these are suited to continuous numeric data measured along a true numeric scale.

blocks.title: Self-check: identify the scale of measurement

items: Sickle cell status (AA, AS, SS) → categories with no inherent order → nominal.
Disease severity (low, medium, high) → ordered categories, but unequal/undefined gaps between them → ordinal.
Body temperature (°C) → ordered, equal intervals, but 0°C does not mean "no temperature" → interval.
Number of hospital visits → ordered, equal intervals, and 0 genuinely means no visits at all → ratio.
